blocks.text: Jory Ashdown watched the far seal turn a quarter round, slow as a man reading small print, and stop dead. Through the pane in Postscript's own hatch he saw Compline's clamps bite the collar ring and stay bitten.
"They've locked it," he said. "Their side. They've not opened it."
"Gam law," said Soph, behind him. "Two hours matched before anything crosses. Technically they're being polite."

"Polite." Jory did not trust a polite ship. Engines told you when they were unhappy. He had left Margaret on the bench aft, and his hands, which were never empty, hung at his sides with nothing to do.

The captain was at the manifest board, not wiping it. That was new. He looked at the Inspector, who stood by the gam lock with one hand still on the rail, and then he said, very evenly, "Waybill. The Hearth haul. Play the Inspector what we heard."
"The captain decides what is played aloud," said Waybill. "Playing my log of that playback."
The cabin filled with the cabin. Hiss of air, the hum of the galley fans, and Jory's own voice, close and tired. "I want it off my ship."
He had heard it before. It was worse now, with the real fans going overhead and the real hiss under them, so that he could not have said where the recording stopped and the ship began.
"Technically, it's evidence. Technically, it's ours."
"Opening it is a fine and an endorsement, Captain."
"I know what it costs."
"Then don't. Please."
"Or let me. I haven't got a licence to lose."
"Nobody opens it. Not yet."
Then the fifth voice, a murmur behind a door, words in it and none of them coming through.
"It stays aboard. My call."
"Noted, and not agreed."
Then only fans.

Jory looked at the Inspector. He knew what a face did when the part it had been waiting for turned up in the wrong crate, and hers was doing it. She had gone the colour of fresh sealant. She did not say anything. She did not take her hand off the rail.
Nobody said much after that. The two hours went the way two hours go when you are bolted to a ship that will not say what it wants. The captain made tea nobody drank.
Then, for the first time, somebody knocked.
"Gam logged," said Waybill. "Two hours, matched factor. Vessel: Compline. They are asking to come aboard."
Peregrine Blott sent Jory aft to watch the drive, with thanks, and opened his own seal.

The tall one from the Lee came through first, grey coat, no badge, the same captain who had called him by name across a cold hull. A younger man followed, carrying a Post cask in both hands as if it were hot. They stopped on the lip of the lock and bowed, a little, the way clerks bow.
"Captain Blott," said the tall one. "Inspector."
"Gentlemen," said Peregrine. "Tea?"
"You're very kind. We shan't stay." The tall one nodded, and the younger one held out the cask. "This is yours."
Peregrine did not take it yet. "Why bring it?"
"Because the Register says we did."
He took it. Shoebox size, Post grey, a little heavier than it looked. He set it in the cask cradle by the manifest board and re-seated the clamp, which for once needed it.
"Waybill. Read the mark."

"Post cask, sealed, seal intact. Postmark: Postscript, ship's reckoning. Calendar: Quarto." Waybill paused, the way it did when two records met. "A little over four years ahead of our reckoning, Captain, by the Almanac. I can give it to the hour."
"Not now."
"Addressee: Captain P. Blott, Postscript. Sender: P. Blott, Postscript. Handed to its addressee aboard, it is judged by this ship's reckoning." Another pause. "Void, Captain. By Precedence."
"Four years on the wrong side of the sun," said Soph, very quietly, from the galley.
Peregrine looked at the address label. The hand was his. Not like his. His, with four more years in the wrist.
So she would fly that long. So would he. Somebody aboard this ship, from this ship's reckoning, would seal that box and send it, and the label said who.
"Thank you for carrying it," he said.
"When you have something for us, Captain," said the tall one, "hand it across. We'll hold the collar."
"And if I haven't anything?"
The tall one smiled, kindly enough. "You have."

They stepped back through the lock. Their own seal wound half shut behind them and stopped there, so that a grey sleeve showed in the gap. Compline did not let go. Peregrine could feel her holding, the way you feel a hand on your shoulder in a crowd.
He stood by the cradle with his palm flat on the clamp and found he was being very polite to nobody at all.
Constance Aubrey stood inside the gam lock with Postscript's hatch half wound at her back, because somebody ought to watch Compline's seal and she was the only person aboard whose job it was.

It had been her voice. She had known it before the second word. Stay with the ship, the note had said, and here she was, with the ship, a line on a card that had arrived before she had ever set foot on the deck. She examined the feeling, found it accurate, and kept watching the seal.
"Inspector." The captain's voice came through the gap behind her. "The grey coats in the Lee were those. They cut your stub off my keel-ring and polished the ring after. That's the story I owed you."
So her evidence had been gone since the Lee. "Thank you, Captain," she said, and filed that beside everything else.
"Then open it," said the Navigator. "Now. Before they come back for it."

Aubrey turned her head, not her body. "Navigator. Before anyone says a thing they'll regret. The Captain's probation hold lapsed unentered at Gnomon, when my inquiry was closed. His licence carries no endorsement. Open a void item in the Drift and it carries one."
A pause. "Nobody told me that."

"Nobody was asked." Aubrey made herself go on. "And a recording of this cabin reached a keel locker nineteen months ago. I have seen the stub of the road it took. If this ship puts anything down that road, I will write it up as using an illicit channel, which is an endorsement. Two suspend a licence."
Nobody spoke. The fans ran. She heard the drive-space hatch, and the Engineer's slow tread come up from aft, and stop.
Then the Engineer said, "I want it off my ship."
Aubrey shut her eyes. There it was. He was not reciting. He meant it, which was worse.
"Technically, it's evidence," said the Navigator. "Technically, it's ours."
"Opening it is a fine and an endorsement, Captain," said Waybill.
"I know what it costs," said the captain.
"Then don't. Please."

There was a gap then, long enough to drive a cart through. Aubrey could not see the Navigator's face, only hear her breathe in, and she understood that the Navigator had heard her own line an hour ago and was choosing it now, knowing.
"Or let me. I haven't got a licence to lose."
"Nobody opens it," said the captain. "Not yet."
Aubrey had no inquiry. She had no warrant. She had a Ravel Desk that had been closed by order and a note in her coat from somebody who knew more than her superiors did. She opened her mouth anyway.
"That cask goes under Inspectorate seal, Captain."
She heard the half-closed hatch take the words and flatten them, the way it had flattened them on the card.
"It stays aboard," said the captain. "My call."

She could have said nothing. Nobody would ever know but Waybill, and Waybill would only know what she had not said. The recording would have ended one line short, and she would have proved something about free will to an empty lock.
She did not want to prove anything. She wanted to be right.
"Noted, and not agreed."
Then only the galley fans. Nobody spoke over them. Waybill had logged every word, as ship's law required, and for a long moment that was the only thing in the cabin doing its job.
Jory Ashdown had sat at a lot of galley tables, but never one with Laurence Prynne's handwriting on it.
"He gave me this at Gnomon," said the captain, and unfolded it.
Soph read it upside down and then the right way up. "You've had that since Gnomon?"
"Yes."

"Void and bother, Captain." But she was already reading. "Ravel moored to our keel-ring at Quarto, the day we left for Hearth. Spool-end tally, one day twenty. Lands in the locker two days twenty into the haul." She tapped the sheet. "That's the Turn. Mooring, plus whatever thread's been run off the spool end, plus a day. So whoever holds the spool end sends at one day twenty on their own clock."
"Them," said Jory, and nodded at the seal.
"Them. And what goes down it is that." She pointed at the speaker grille, where the fans still were. "This. Us. The card."
"We've spools," said Jory, though he knew better.
"Waybill?"
"Post spools aboard: none."

"And a tether only goes home to the port you moored it at," said Soph. "Theirs is the only road that runs back to Quarto nineteen months ago. We send it down their line or it never got there, and it got there."
Jory sat with that. He was slow; it was why his welds held. He turned the extract round and looked at the two numbers on it the way he looked at a pressure curve.

"Nineteen months of ground," he said, "and not two days of thread." He laughed once, early, at a joke he had not finished making. "Nothing we build runs like that. Not Postscript, not the Board, not the Combine's best. That spool end's been somewhere running deeper than anything I've ever had my hands in."

And then he saw the rest of it, all at once, like a crack you notice only when the light goes across it. The grey coats had cut the keel-ring clean in the Lee. They would do the same to Waybill's logs, sooner or later, and to anything else aboard that remembered. But there was one thing they could never touch, because it was not aboard. The Hearth cask sat in the Inspector's evidence locker, sealed since Saltpan, lining never looked at. It had already arrived. Whatever was in it had always been in it.
"Engineer," said the captain, "would you fetch a cask from stores and check the seal ring for me?"
"Aye, Captain."
He took it aft to the drive space and set it on the bench, and picked up the spanner. "Right, Margaret," he said. "You and me." The Bishop sat in its clip and watched.

He found a fuel docket in his top pocket, soft with handling, and a pencil stub. For the Inspector's locker, he wrote at the top, small, the way he wrote torque settings. Then the rest of it, small and tight, ending on the bearing of Compline's approach, which he copied figure for figure from Waybill's sensor log. He signed it with his initials.
He lifted the cask's lining at one corner with Margaret's thin end, slid the docket flat beneath it, and pressed the lining down until it lay as if it had never moved.
"Easy, Margaret," he said.
The seal ring was perfect. He carried the cask forward.
Constance Aubrey watched the captain take the card from Waybill's slot.
"Cut from the Engineer's first line to the fans," Waybill said. "Signed. Keyed to the keel."
The captain laid it in the cask Jory had brought, closed the lid, and sealed it with his own hand, there in the cabin, with the drive running under them.

"Sealed under drive, by crew," said Waybill. "Postmark: Postscript, ship's reckoning. Calendar: Folio. Sender: Postscript. Addressee: Postscript. Mass at sealing: one thousand nine hundred and six grams." It paused. "That matches the cask received in the keel locker on the Hearth haul. To the gram."
Aubrey had impounded that cask. She had written that number in her own evidence log at Saltpan.
The Navigator frowned at the cask, and then at the Engineer. "A card weighs nothing."
The Engineer looked at the Bishop, which had nothing to say either. Aubrey filed his silence where she kept the others.
The captain carried the cask to the lock and handed it through the gap. A grey sleeve took it. Nobody on the other side said a word.

Aubrey took out her notebook and wrote, in front of him, so that he could read it upside down if he cared to. Captain P. Blott, Second Class. Sent a cask down a ravel moored and held by others. The lesser offence: use of an illicit channel. Endorsable.
She read it to him aloud. It seemed only fair.
"Thank you, Inspector," he said.
"It goes in when I reach a desk that will take it."
"I know."
"How long," she said, before she could decide not to, "have you known that voice was mine?"
He thought about it, which she appreciated. "Since the bees."
"Collar released," said Waybill. "Compline has broken the gam."

Through the port Aubrey watched the long dark hull fall away, carrying a box she had just watched sealed that had sat in her locker for well over a year. She found she was not angry. She was something else, and she did not yet have the Code's word for it.
Soph Vell wanted that cask open more than she had wanted anything since the academy, and she was not ashamed of it, and she was not going to touch it.
It sat in the hold, logged and strapped, Post grey, perfectly ordinary. She had walked past it more often on the haul home to Quarto than she cared to admit.
"Leave it be," said Jory, from under a panel.
"I am leaving it be. I'm leaving it be out loud." She sat on the step with her knees up. "It's void aboard. So only a counter can stamp it RETURNED. Agreed?"
"Agreed."
"And only its sender opens it after that. Sender's crew aboard this ship, so the Code sends it to the ship's next filing office and puts it in his hand there. In person. At the counter."
"Which is Quarto," said Jory.
"Which is Quarto, where we're going anyway, which is either convenient or sinister." She glared at the cask. "And the mark's on Quarto's calendar. Do you see what that means?"
Jory came out from under the panel. "Tell me slow."

"Ship's reckoning is the last port you filed at, plus hull time. Quarto calendar means that in four years, the last place we file before somebody seals that box under drive is Quarto." She swallowed. "Us. Him. This ship. We're going to be here. We're going to still be flying her."
Jory thought about that. Then he smiled, slowly, the way he smiled at an engine that had decided to behave. "Four more years of you arguing with my drive."
"Don't."
But she was smiling too.

The captain came down the ladder for a strap tensioner and went past the cask without looking at it. She had watched him do that the whole haul, hull hour after hull hour, and never once touch it. On the Hearth haul he had broken a seal because he could not bear not to know.
He had learned that much, then. So had she, apparently. She had not decided yet whether she liked it.
Peregrine Blott docked at Quarto in grace and carried the run's last Post bag up to the counter himself.
Ko was behind it, with garden soil on his cuffs and his reading glasses on his forehead. He weighed the bag, read the bill, checked the hour against his drawer, and punched it.
"Tenth of ten, Cadet," he said. "Valid, punched, and well inside its hour. That's your run."
"Run complete," said Peregrine. It came out plain. He let it.
Behind him Soph and Jory had found reasons to stand near the door. The Inspector had not bothered to find one; she simply stood there.
Peregrine set the grey cask on the counter. "One more. For tender."
Ko lowered his glasses and read the mark. He read it twice. Then he set it against his drawer's edition, as he would have for anyone, and his face did nothing at all.
"Void," he said. "By a little over four years." He reached under the counter for the purple pad and struck the stamp down once, hard, square. RETURNED.

He turned the cask to the lamp and read the sender line aloud, as the Code required. "P. Blott, Postscript." He looked up. "Your ship is filing at this counter, Captain. Returned post goes into its sender's hand. In person." He slid the cask across. "A letter that comes home has nothing to be ashamed of."
Peregrine put both hands on it.

On the Hearth haul he had broken a seal in the dark of his own hold because he could not stand not knowing. This seal he broke at a Post Office counter, under a lamp, in front of a postmaster, his crew and an Inspector, and it was the most lawful thing he had ever done with his hands.
The seal bloomed purple and let go.

Inside, wrapped in a square of ship's cloth, was a courier licence. His. Same name, same number, the corners rounded off by four more years in somebody's coat. Through the middle, clean as a clerk could make it, a punch, and round the punch in red: VOID. The date beside it was four years from today.
He took his own licence out of his coat and laid it beside the other one on the counter. Nobody said anything. Soph made a small sound and stopped it.

Under the cloth there was something else. A short, ugly coil of tether thread, dead and grey, fused to a sliver of dark metal that had been cut, not broken, from the curve of a keel-ring. A stub. On the sliver, cut deep and old, the way the Post stamped things it meant to last, was a sigil: a half-circle of fine ticks round one upright stroke, like a clock that kept time by shadow.
Nobody at the counter said they knew it.
Peregrine turned the sliver to the lamp, and asked the one question nobody wanted asked. "Whose keel was this cut from?"
